lead: A V-belt sits in a grooved pulley and wedges into it. The wedge raises the effective friction from μ to about μ / sin β, roughly three times, so the drive grips with a short centre distance and small pulleys. The price is that one belt carries only a few kilowatts; the drive is rated as a number of standard belts. V-belts run pumps, compressors, fans and machine tools, including many Indian workshop drives.
prereq: You need 6.2 for the tension ratio and power relation, and 6.1 for belt construction.

blocks.text: A flat belt grips only on the pulley rim. A V-belt grips on its two side faces, which press against the sides of a groove. The wedge action makes the normal force larger than the belt pull, so the friction that can be developed is larger. The same tension ratio as a flat belt applies, with μ replaced by the effective friction μ′.

blocks.where: β is the half groove angle; μ is the real coefficient of friction between belt and pulley; μ′ is the effective friction.
T<sub>1</sub> is tight-side tension in N; T<sub>2</sub> is slack-side tension in N; T<sub>c</sub> is centrifugal tension in N; θ is arc of contact on the small pulley in radians; e = 2.718.

blocks.text: For 2β = 38°, β = 19°, sin 19° = 0.326, so μ′ ≈ 3.07 μ. This is why a V-drive can use a centre distance shorter than a flat-belt drive and a small pulley that would slip with a flat belt. Groove angle is 34° to 40°; small pulleys use the narrower angle so the belt still bears on both sides after bending. A V-flat drive runs a V-belt on one grooved pulley and one flat pulley; it is used for quarter-turn drives and reversing, but the flat pulley gives less grip.

V-belts come in standard sections. The letter gives the cross-section; the number gives the pitch length in millimetres. Thus B 1000 is a B-section belt with pitch length 1000 mm. Pitch length is measured on the pitch line, the line inside the belt that does not change length when the belt bends.

Larger sections carry more power but need larger pulleys. For a first choice, use a selection chart that plots kW against small-pulley speed for each section. The belt speed is v = π d N / 60, where d is the small pulley pitch diameter in metres, N is its speed in rev/min, and v is in m/s. Keep v ≤ 25 m/s. Above this, centrifugal tension T<sub>c</sub> = m v² becomes large, where m is belt mass per metre; grip falls and the belt flexes too often.

A smaller section can run on a smaller pulley and at higher speed, but needs more belts. Do not mix sections on one pulley set. Tensioning is by sliding the motor on rails or by an idler; check deflection at mid-span.

Design starts with the duty. The service factor F<sub>a</sub> accounts for shock and running hours. Design power P<sub>d</sub> = F<sub>a</sub> P, where P is the motor power in kW and P<sub>d</sub> is the power the belts must be rated for. A smooth electric motor driving a compressor for two shifts may need F<sub>a</sub> = 1.2; a crusher may need 1.5 or more.

items: Choose section from P<sub>d</sub> and speed.
Choose small pulley above the minimum for the section; find large pulley from ratio.
Read rated power P<sub>r</sub> per belt at the small-pulley speed and diameter.
Find arc factor K<sub>θ</sub> and length factor K<sub>L</sub>.
N = P<sub>d</sub> / (P<sub>r</sub> K<sub>θ</sub> K<sub>L</sub>); round up.

blocks.where: N is number of belts; P<sub>d</sub> is design power in kW; P<sub>r</sub> is rated power per belt in kW; K<sub>θ</sub> is arc of contact factor; K<sub>L</sub> is belt length factor.

blocks.text: P<sub>r</sub> is from a chart for 180° arc and standard length. K<sub>θ</sub> is below 1 when θ is less than 180°, as with a speed reduction. K<sub>L</sub> is below 1 for a belt shorter than the standard; a short belt bends more times per second. Round N up; keep N ≤ about 8. If N is larger, use a bigger section, larger pulleys or two drives. More belts share load unevenly unless they are matched and tensioned together.

figure.caption: The design flow from required power to the number of belts; the last box is the rounded-up count.

spec.aria: A six-step flowchart from design power to the number of V-belts, passing through section choice, pulley diameters, rated power and correction factors.

examples.question: A 7.5 kW, 1440 rpm motor drives a reciprocating compressor at 480 rpm for two shifts of 8 h a day. Select a B-section V-belt drive with pitch diameters 140 mm and 420 mm and centre distance 420 mm. The rating chart gives 2.6 kW per belt; arc factor is 0.87 and length factor 0.95. Take service factor 1.2. Find the number of belts.
steps: Design power P<sub>d</sub> = F<sub>a</sub> P = 1.2 × 7.5 = 9.0 kW.
Belt speed v = π d N<sub>1</sub> / 60 = π × 0.140 × 1440 / 60 = 10.56 m/s, below 25 m/s.
Corrected rating per belt = P<sub>r</sub> K<sub>θ</sub> K<sub>L</sub> = 2.6 × 0.87 × 0.95 = 2.149 kW.
examples.check:
import math
P=7.5
Fa=1.2
Pd=P*Fa
N1=1440
d=0.140
D=0.420
C=0.420
v=math.pi*d*N1/60
alpha=math.degrees(math.asin((D-d)/(2*C)))
theta=180-2*alpha
Pr=2.6
Kt=0.87
KL=0.95
Pr_corr=Pr*Kt*KL
N=Pd/Pr_corr
chosen=math.ceil(N)
print(f"{Pd:.2f}")
print(f"{v:.2f}")
print(f"{alpha:.2f}")
print(f"{theta:.2f}")
print(f"{Pr_corr:.3f}")
print(f"{N:.2f}")
print(chosen)

traps: Using the full groove angle 2β in sin β. If 2β = 38°, β = 19°, so sin β = sin 19° = 0.326, not sin 38° = 0.616. The wrong value roughly halves μ′ and oversizes the drive.
Forgetting the service factor. P is motor output, P<sub>d</sub> = F<sub>a</sub> P is what the belts must carry. Using P directly undersizes the drive.
Using millimetres in v = π d N / 60. Put d in metres; 140 mm is 0.140 m. Mixing units gives a speed 1000 times too large.
Rounding the number of belts down. 4.19 belts means 5 belts; 4 belts are overloaded.
Using the flat-belt tension ratio e<sup>(μθ)</sup> for a V-belt. The V-belt ratio uses μ / sin β, about three times larger.

quiz.q: What does the designation B 1000 mean?
Why does a V-belt carry more power than a flat belt of the same width?
quiz.a: The V-belt wedges into the groove, so the normal force on the side faces is larger. Effective friction is μ / sin β, about three times μ for β = 19°.

quiz.q: A V-belt has μ = 0.3 and half groove angle β = 19°. Find μ′.
Why does the groove angle narrow on small pulleys?
quiz.a: The belt bends around a small pulley and its sides tend to open. A narrower groove keeps both side faces in contact, so the wedge and friction are maintained.

quiz.q: Find belt speed for d = 100 mm and N = 1500 rpm.
The calculated number of belts is 7.6. What do you do?
quiz.a: Round up to 8 belts. Eight is at the usual limit; if the count were above 8, use a larger section, larger pulleys or two drives.

quiz.q: Why is the length factor below 1 for a short belt?
quiz.a: A short belt bends more times per second for the same speed, so it fatigues faster and its rated power is reduced.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses standard selection charts, raw-edge cogged belts and variable-speed V-belt drives; tension gauges and vibration checks set the take-up. V-flat and multi-groove drives are common on fans and pumps. Search 'V-belt drive selection ISO 4184', 'V-flat drive' and 'belt tension gauge'.
